items.title: Finite products of dominated kernels have the product density
items.statement: Let n be a positive integer and let S be a common source space. For each j<n, let K_j be a probability kernel from S to T_j with a specified jointly measurable density f_j with respect to a sigma-finite measure nu_j. The finite product kernel has density L(s,t)=product_j f_j(s,t_j) with respect to the finite product measure product_j nu_j.
items.axiom_use: None. The product is finite; the product-kernel, sigma-finite product-measure, Tonelli, and finite-measure uniqueness arguments use no choice axiom.

references.title: Andrew Gelman, John B. Carlin, Hal S. Stern, David B. Dunson, Aki Vehtari, and Donald B. Rubin, Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §5.3
Alicia A. Johnson, Miles Q. Ott, and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapters 15–16

items.title: Finite-group hierarchical Bayesian model
items.statement: Fix a finite group count m>=1, standard Borel hyperparameter and parameter spaces H and Theta, a proper hyperprior Pi on H, and a jointly measurable probability kernel eta -> G_eta on Theta. For each group j, let K_j be a probability kernel from Theta to an observation space Y_j, dominated by a sigma-finite measure nu_j with specified jointly measurable density f_j. The model draws eta from Pi, draws theta_1,...,theta_m conditionally independently from G_eta, and draws the group observations conditionally independently from K_j(theta_j,·). Its latent prior is P0(deta,dtheta_1:m)=Pi(deta) product_j G_eta(dtheta_j); its observation density is L_y(eta,theta_1:m)=product_j f_j(theta_j,y_j); its evidence is Z(y)=integral L_y dP0. A normalized posterior is defined only when 0<Z(y)<infinity. The product-kernel structure is an explicit modeling assumption; an arbitrary finitely exchangeable law need not be a mixture of iid laws, and no finite de Finetti theorem is claimed.
items.axiom_use: The finite product-kernel construction is choice-free. AC is included only for the library's conditional-independence terminology, whose definition uses conditional-expectation classes; no de Finetti or infinite exchangeability result is used.

references.title: Andrew Gelman, John B. Carlin, Hal S. Stern, David B. Dunson, Aki Vehtari, and Donald B. Rubin, Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §§5.1–5.4
Alicia A. Johnson, Miles Q. Ott, and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapters 15–16

items.title: A finite-group hierarchical model has a conditional law of its latent tuple
items.statement: Assume AC and the hypotheses of the finite-group hierarchical model definition. On the canonical joint probability space, the latent tuple (eta,theta_1,...,theta_m) has a regular conditional distribution given the sigma-algebra generated by the observed data. It is a probability kernel at every sample point, including exceptional points; this existence statement alone does not identify a normalized likelihood posterior on a fixed observation fiber where evidence is zero or infinite.
items.axiom_use: AC is used exactly when applying the standard-Borel regular-conditional-distribution existence theorem. Finite products of standard-Borel spaces and the joint-kernel construction are choice-free.

references.title: Andrew Gelman, John B. Carlin, Hal S. Stern, David B. Dunson, Aki Vehtari, and Donald B. Rubin, Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §§5.2–5.3
Alicia A. Johnson, Miles Q. Ott, and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapter 16

items.title: Hierarchical posterior normalization on positive finite evidence
items.statement: Assume the finite-group hierarchical model and write P0 for its proper latent prior, L_y for its product likelihood density, and Z(y)=integral L_y dP0. For every observation y with 0<Z(y)<infinity, the measure P_y(A)=integral_A L_y dP0 / Z(y) is the posterior law of the latent tuple. Setting P_y=P0 on fibers with Z(y)=0 or Z(y)=infinity gives a regular conditional distribution under the prior-predictive law; no quotient is formed on those exceptional fibers.
items.axiom_use: The normalization and conditional-density calculation are choice-free. The model's conditional-independence terminology and the separately stated RCD-existence branch carry the AC assumption explicitly.

references.title: Andrew Gelman, John B. Carlin, Hal S. Stern, David B. Dunson, Aki Vehtari, and Donald B. Rubin, Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §§5.2–5.3
Alicia A. Johnson, Miles Q. Ott, and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapter 16

items.title: Conditional normal shrinkage in a finite hierarchy
items.statement:
Assume the normal specialization of [[def-hierarchical-bayesian-model]] with
parameter space $\Theta=\mathbb R$ and hyperparameter space
$H=\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)$. Fix $\mu\in\mathbb R$ and $\tau^2>0$.
Conditional on $(\mu,\tau^2)$, let the
group parameters be independent with $\theta_j\sim N(\mu,\tau^2)$. Let the
observed group summaries be conditionally independent with
$\bar Y_j\mid\theta_j\sim N(\theta_j,s_j^2)$, where each known $s_j^2>0$. In this normal specialization, the supplied
likelihood-density version is the canonical normal density at every parameter
and observation value:
$$f_j(\theta,y)=(2\pi s_j^2)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(y-\theta)^2}{2s_j^2}\right)\qquad(\theta,y\in\mathbb R).$$
Then, conditional on $(\mu,\tau^2,\bar Y_1=\bar y_1,\ldots,\bar Y_m=\bar y_m)$,
the $\theta_j$ are independent and
$$\theta_j\sim N(\hat\theta_j,V_j),\qquad\hat\theta_j=\frac{\bar y_j/s_j^2+\mu/\tau^2}{1/s_j^2+1/\tau^2},\qquad V_j=\left(1/s_j^2+1/\tau^2\right)^{-1}.$$
If $(\mu,\tau^2)$ is unknown with a proper hyperprior supported on
$\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)$, let $P_y$ be the full posterior kernel from
[[thm-hierarchical-posterior-normalization-on-positive-finite-evidence]] and,
on each positive finite evidence fiber, define its hyperparameter marginal on
Borel $C\subseteq H$ by $\Pi_y(C):=P_y(C\times\mathbb R^m)$. The posterior law of
$\theta_j$ is the mixture of these conditional normal laws over $\Pi_y$;
replacing $\mu,\tau^2$ by point estimates need not give this posterior. No normalized
hyperparameter posterior is asserted on a zero or infinite evidence fiber.
items.axiom_use: AC is used through the Gaussian-normalization hypothesis in the BCS-03 Normal–Normal update and through the hierarchy's conditional-independence terminology. The finite-product factorization and hyperparameter mixture use no additional choice principle.

references.title: Andrew Gelman, John B. Carlin, Hal S. Stern, David B. Dunson, Aki Vehtari, and Donald B. Rubin, Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §5.4
Alicia A. Johnson, Miles Q. Ott, and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapters 15–16

items.title: Current-group and new-group posterior prediction
items.statement: On a positive-finite evidence fiber with latent posterior Pi_y, define the current-group predictive law for group j by mixing its observation kernel K_j(theta_j,·) over Pi_y. Define the new-group predictive law by first mixing K_new(theta,·) over the population kernel G_eta and then mixing that resulting law over Pi_y. The current-group law uses the posterior of the already observed theta_j; the new-group law first draws a new latent parameter from G_eta. Both predictions retain uncertainty in eta and the group parameters.
items.axiom_use: The kernel mixtures are choice-free. AC is inherited only through the conditional-expectation-class convention in the cited regular-conditional integration result.

references.title: Andrew Gelman, John B. Carlin, Hal S. Stern, David B. Dunson, Aki Vehtari, and Donald B. Rubin, Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §5.4
Alicia A. Johnson, Miles Q. Ott, and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapter 16, §16.5

items.title: Current-group and new-group posterior predictions are probability kernels
items.statement: Under the finite-group hierarchical model and on the measurable set of observations with positive finite evidence, the current-group and new-group posterior predictive assignments are probability kernels. Integrating over an existing group uses its latent posterior; integrating over a new group first uses G_eta and then the posterior of eta. The resulting kernels satisfy the conditional-integration identities for future observations.
items.axiom_use: The sectionwise probability-kernel and measurability checks are choice-free. AC is used only for the inherited conditional-expectation-class interpretation in regular-conditional integration.

references.title: Andrew Gelman, John B. Carlin, Hal S. Stern, David B. Dunson, Aki Vehtari, and Donald B. Rubin, Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §5.4
Alicia A. Johnson, Miles Q. Ott, and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapter 16, §16.5

title: Hierarchical Bayes and partial pooling — Examples

items.title: An improper variance hyperprior can give an improper posterior
items.statement: In the one-group normal hierarchy theta|t~N(0,t), Y|theta~N(theta,1), observe y=0 and replace the proper hyperprior by the improper density pi(t) proportional to 1/t on t>0. After integrating theta out, the evidence-weighted density for t is proportional to 1/(t sqrt(1+t)), whose integral diverges at zero. Therefore the joint posterior cannot be normalized; the example is outside the proper-hyperprior theorem's hypotheses.
items.axiom_use: AC is inherited only through the library normal-law convention; the Gaussian integral and divergence calculation are choice-free.

references.title: Andrew Gelman, John B. Carlin, Hal S. Stern, David B. Dunson, Aki Vehtari, and Donald B. Rubin, Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §5.7
Alicia A. Johnson, Miles Q. Ott, and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapter 16

items.title: Integrating hyperparameter uncertainty versus plugging in
items.statement:
Let the hyperparameter be $t=\tau^2\in\{1,4\}$ with prior probability
$1/2$ at each value. There is one group, $\theta\mid t\sim N(0,t)$, and
$Y\mid\theta\sim N(\theta,1)$. Observe $y=0$. Specify the likelihood-density version pointwise by
$$f(\theta,y)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\exp(-(y-\theta)^2/2)\qquad(\theta,y\in\mathbb R).$$
The full posterior for $\theta$
is a mixture of the two conditional normal posteriors. Plugging in the
posterior mode of $t$ instead yields just one component, which is not the full
posterior.
items.axiom_use: AC is inherited through the library normal-law and conditional-expectation conventions; the finite mixture and Gaussian integral calculations are choice-free.

references.title: Andrew Gelman, John B. Carlin, Hal S. Stern, David B. Dunson, Aki Vehtari, and Donald B. Rubin, Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §§5.3–5.4
Alicia A. Johnson, Miles Q. Ott, and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapter 16

items.title: Complete, partial, and no-pooling limits in the normal hierarchy
items.statement:
In the known-variance normal hierarchy, fix $\mu$, an observed group summary
$\bar y_j$, and $s_j^2>0$. Specify the likelihood-density version pointwise by
$$f_j(\theta,y)=(2\pi s_j^2)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(y-\theta)^2}{2s_j^2}\right)\qquad(\theta,y\in\mathbb R).$$
For finite $\tau^2>0$, the posterior mean is a
strictly weighted average of $\bar y_j$ and $\mu$. As $\tau^2\downarrow0$ it
approaches complete pooling at $\mu$; at the boundary $\tau^2=0$, the prior
itself forces $\theta_j=\mu$. As $\tau^2\to\infty$, the posterior mean and
variance approach the group-only values $\bar y_j$ and $s_j^2$, the
no-pooling limit. The value $\tau^2=\infty$ is not an admissible proper prior.
items.axiom_use: AC is inherited only through the library normal-law definition used for the degenerate boundary; the weight and limit calculations are choice-free.

references.title: Andrew Gelman, John B. Carlin, Hal S. Stern, David B. Dunson, Aki Vehtari, and Donald B. Rubin, Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §5.4
Alicia A. Johnson, Miles Q. Ott, and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapters 15–16
